title: 4.2-kiloyear drought event

facts.text: A severe drought began about 4,200 years ago; starting around 2200 BC it probably lasted the whole 22nd century BC, among the Holocene's harshest climate events.
Intense aridity is recorded from North Africa and the Middle East to Arabia, India and midcontinental North America; the East Asian summer monsoon weakened sharply.
Models link it to a major weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation, and the tropical rain belt (ITCZ) shifted abruptly south.
It is thought to have helped topple Egypt's Old Kingdom, the Akkadian Empire and China's Liangzhu culture, as Nile floods failed and irrigated fields salted up.
A Mawmluh Cave stalagmite in India marks it as the Meghalayan's base, 4,250 years before 2000; critics argue the drought was neither global nor neatly timed.

contested_note: Its use as the Meghalayan's base is debated, since critics say the drought was neither global nor confined to a clear timeframe.

title: Last woolly mammoths die on Wrangel Island

facts.text: A small population of dwarf woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island, in the Siberian Arctic, until about 4,000 years ago.
They outlasted mainland mammoths by some 6,000 years and were the last mammoths anywhere.
The latest Wrangel remains are dated to 1795–1675 BCE.
Their extinction did not coincide with human arrival; the island had been a human-free refuge.

title: Humid period ends in East and equatorial Africa

facts.text: A major pan-tropical environmental change took place about 4,000 years ago; drying in East Africa peaked around then.
Blue Nile discharge fell noticeably, and its sediment load rose as vegetation thinned in the catchment from 4,000–3,600 years ago.
In the Sahara, Lake Teli dried out completely about 4,200 years ago, and groundwater-fed Lake Yoa turned hypersaline by 4,000 years ago.
Nearer the equator the humid period ended later, between 4,000 and 2,500 years ago; West Africa had a long dry phase 3,500–1,700 years ago.
South of the equator, at Lake Malawi, drying began only about 1,000 years ago.
About 1860 BCE Mount St. Helens laid down its Yn (Smith Creek) tephra in a VEI 6 eruption of roughly 15 km³.

facts.text: Around 1800 BC Vesuvius erupted in the VEI 6 Avellino eruption, one of at least three prehistoric eruptions much larger than that of AD 79.
It destroyed several Bronze Age settlements; near Nola a hastily abandoned village and thousands of fleeing footprints were buried under pumice and ash.
Pyroclastic surges travelled 15 km northwest of the vent, leaving deposits up to 3 m deep where Naples now stands.

title: Weakening monsoon dries the Indus valley

facts.text: From about 1800 BCE the Indus Valley grew markedly cooler and drier as the monsoon weakened.
The monsoon-fed Ghaggar-Hakra rivers became seasonal around 4,000 years ago as the Indus civilisation waned; most of its cities were abandoned by about 1700 BCE.
The Indian summer monsoon stayed weaker from 3,510 to 2,550 BP, apart from a strong interval 3,400–3,200 BP.

title: Aniakchak eruption and the 1627 BC cold

facts.text: Alaska's Mount Aniakchak erupted at VEI 6, ejecting about 50 km³ of material; a 2019 revised Greenland ice-core chronology dates it to 1628 BC.
Ash in a major Greenland sulfate spike, long blamed on Thera, was matched to Aniakchak instead.
Frost-damaged tree rings record extreme global cooling in 1627 BC, now attributed to Aniakchak.

title: Minoan eruption of Thera (Santorini)

facts.text: A catastrophic Plinian eruption devastated the Aegean island of Thera (Santorini) around 1600 BC, leaving the caldera that forms its central bay.
Rated VEI 7, it ejected about 28–41 km³ dense-rock equivalent, one of the largest volcanic events in human history.
It destroyed Minoan Akrotiri and, with earthquakes and tsunamis, struck nearby islands and the coast of Crete.
Its ash is a marker layer at nearly every eastern Mediterranean site; Chinese annals of yellow skies and summer frost may record its volcanic winter.

contested_note: Its exact date has been fiercely debated for decades: radiocarbon favours the 17th–16th century BC, archaeology about 1550–1480 BC.

title: Last ground sloths vanish from the Caribbean

facts.text: Caribbean ground sloths, the group's last survivors, lived on Cuba, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico possibly until 1550 BCE.
Mainland ground sloths had died out about 11,000 years ago; the island relicts outlived them, much as Wrangel Island's mammoths did.

title: Last litopterns may die out

facts.text: Litopterns, an order of South American native hoofed mammals that arose 62.5 million years ago, are usually thought to have vanished about 12,000 years ago.
A 2025 study of a Xenorhinotherium specimen radiocarbon dated to 3,493–4,217 years ago suggests the order survived into the late Holocene.

contested_note: Survival to about 3,500 years ago rests on a single 2025 radiocarbon date; the usual end date is about 12,000 years ago.

title: Kaali meteorite craters form in Estonia

facts.text: A meteor of 20–80 tonnes broke up in the air and blasted nine craters on Saaremaa, Estonia; the largest is 110 m across.
The blast incinerated vegetation up to 6 km away; it is one of the few impacts in a populated area.
The latest estimates place it shortly after 1530–1450 BC, though published ages vary by up to 6,000 years.

title: Thylacine and devil vanish from mainland Australia

facts.text: The consensus is that thylacines died out on mainland Australia around 1277–1229 BCE; the latest mainland Tasmanian devil remains share that date.
Competition with human hunters and dingoes is the likely cause, with a warming climate also proposed.
Both survived only in Tasmania, long before European settlement.

facts.text: Hekla's H3 eruption, one of Iceland's largest of the Holocene, threw about 7.3 km³ of rock into the atmosphere, a VEI 5 event.
Its traces reach Scottish peat bogs, Hekla's big prehistoric eruptions left date-marker layers across northern Europe, and Irish tree rings show a decade of stunted growth.
It probably cooled the northern parts of the globe for a few years; recalibrated with IntCal20, it dates to 1063 ± 140 BCE.

facts.text: A deep, persistent grand solar minimum, the Homeric Minimum, lasted from about 800 to 600 BC.
It is linked to the Homeric Climate Oscillation, or 2.8 kyr event, when western North America and Europe grew colder; whether wetter or drier is debated.
Germany's Meerfelder Maar records a lasting shift to colder, wetter, windier weather, and the Göschenen I glacier advance in the Alps relates to it.

title: Central Sahara becomes a lasting desert

facts.text: By 2,700 years ago the central Sahara had become a desert, which it has remained ever since.
At Libya's Wadi Tanezzuft, water stored in dunes and the Tassili mountains kept rivers flowing until 2,700 years ago, when they finally stopped.
Arabia's long drying trend, under way since 7,000–5,000 years ago, continued until 2,700 years ago.
Brief humid spells still returned, as in Roman North Africa and around the Dead Sea between 500 BCE and 300 CE.
At the Tanezzuft oasis, the drying trend after 1,600 years ago helped end the Garamantian civilisation.

title: Raoul Island eruption forms Denham caldera

facts.text: About 2,200 years ago a major dacitic explosion on Raoul Island, in the Kermadecs, formed the 6.5 by 4 km Denham caldera.
Rated VEI 6 and about the size of Krakatoa's 1883 eruption, it left the Fleetwood tephra; at one spot 40 m of pumice lies under 80 m of ignimbrite.

sources.title: List of large Holocene volcanic eruptions

facts.text: Unusually warm weather prevailed in Europe and the North Atlantic from about 250 BC to AD 400, the Roman Warm Period or Roman Climatic Optimum.
Alpine glaciers show AD 100–400 was markedly warmer than the centuries around it, and Iceland had a warm spell from 230 BC to AD 140.
A 2019 analysis of a much larger proxy dataset found it was a regional phenomenon, not a globally coherent episode.

title: Lake Chad's Bodélé basin dries out

facts.text: Lake Chad shrank to about 5% of its former size; its deep northern Bodélé basin dried out completely about 2,000–1,000 years ago, cut off from the Chari River.
The dry Bodélé basin is today the largest single source of dust on Earth.

title: Madagascar's megafauna dies out after people arrive

facts.text: At least 17 giant lemur species vanished, nearly all after people colonised Madagascar about 2,000 years ago; cut-marked bones show humans by 350 BCE, Bornean Austronesians by 500 CE.
The largest animals vanished soon after people arrived; others fell to prolonged hunting as settlers spread about 1,000 years ago, when areas now lemurless held 20 or more lemur species.
Malagasy hippos and elephant birds are thought to have died out in 750–1050 AD; the youngest Aepyornis maximus remains date to 1040–1380 CE, hippos to 1,000–400 years ago.
Giant lemurs survived into modern times: Megaladapis to 630 ± 50 BP, Palaeopropithecus to 510 ± 80 BP, making this one of history's most recent megafaunal extinctions.
Aridification began nearly 3,000 years ago, and human-set fires deforested the island; on Nosy Be, rainforest became fire-disturbed grassland and woodland 1,300–1,000 years ago.

title: Okmok II eruption and the 43 BCE cold

facts.text: Alaska's Okmok volcano had its second Holocene caldera-forming eruption, rated VEI 6, in 43 BCE.
It sent about 15–16 teragrams of sulfur into the stratosphere, cooling the Northern Hemisphere by 0.7–7.4 °C.
With another eruption a year or two earlier, it made 43 BCE and the next two years among the coldest of the last 2,500 years.
Cold, famine and failed Nile floods followed; this may have helped end Ptolemaic Egypt amid Rome's crisis, though a direct link is unproven.
Its tephra is a time marker in Greenland ice cores, and a lake filled the new caldera within a decade.

title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
article: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD

facts.text: Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, a VEI 5 event of about 3.2 km³ that killed more than 2,000 people.
The eruption that destroyed Pompeii is the benchmark against which other Plinian eruptions are compared.
Collapsing eruption columns sent pyroclastic currents over Herculaneum and Pompeii; Oplontis and Stabiae were also destroyed, and no later Vesuvius eruption was as large.

facts.text: Taupō Volcano's most recent major eruption, the Hatepe, is dated to 232 CE ± 10, partly by wiggle-matching rings of a tree it killed.
It ejected roughly 100–120 km³ of material, 30 km³ within a few minutes, making it one of the largest eruptions of the last 5,000 years.
Its pyroclastic flow was hot enough to burn forest 160 km from Lake Taupō.
It struck before people settled New Zealand; afterwards Lake Taupō refilled and expanded, and temporary lakes formed in the Reporoa basin.

facts.text: Lake Ilopango in El Salvador produced the Tierra Blanca Joven eruption around 430 CE, a VEI 6 event of an estimated 37–82 km³.
It ranks among the most intense eruptions of the Holocene, alongside Thera, Cerro Blanco and Tambora.
Some evidence made Ilopango the source of the 539/540 eruption of the Late Antique Little Ice Age, but a newer study dates it to 431.

facts.text: Extreme weather in 535–536 CE ranks among the notable climate events in Earth history.
It is attributed to a large eruption of unknown source around 536, rated VEI 6–7.
Its climate impact is compared with Tambora in 1815, Samalas in 1257 and the 1452/1453 mystery eruption.
A violent eruption of Krakatoa in 535 was once proposed as the cause, but drilling in the Sunda Strait ruled out an eruption there that year.
Tree rings show the sharpest cold in mid-July to early August 536 across North America and Eurasia; European summers fell up to 2.5 °C below normal.

sources.title: List of large Holocene volcanic eruptions

facts.text: A century-long Northern Hemisphere cooling lasted from AD 536 to about 660, beginning with the volcanic winter of 536.
It coincided with three large eruptions, in 535/536, 539/540 and 547; one study suggests a global cooling of 2 °C.
The second eruption cut European summer temperatures by up to 2.7 °C in 539–540; sea-ice feedback and a deep solar minimum in the 600s prolonged the cold.
Scandinavia may have lost up to half its population, and the cooling coincided with the Plague of Justinian, which began in 541.
It strained the Eastern Roman and Sassanid empires and contributed to the migrations of the Lombards and early Slavs.

title: Mount Churchill's White River Ash eruption

facts.text: Alaska's Mount Churchill erupted at VEI 6 around 847 CE, ejecting about 50 km³ and laying the eastern lobe of the White River Ash.
An earlier VEI 6 eruption about 145–345 CE laid the northern lobe; the ash blankets north-western Canada.

facts.text: In 946 CE Paektu (Baekdu) Mountain, on the China–North Korea border, produced the VEI 6 'Millennium eruption'.
It ranks with Thera, Hatepe, Samalas and Tambora among the largest eruptions of the last few thousand years.
Tree rings counted from the 774–775 Miyake carbon spike and Greenland ice-core tephra fix it to late 946; ashfall records from Nara suggest it began about 2 November.

facts.text: A warm spell, the Medieval Warm Period or Medieval Climate Anomaly, lasted from about 950 to 1250, just before the Little Ice Age.
The Indo-Pacific Warm Pool stayed warm and saline from 1000 to 1400, with temperatures close to today's, then cooled.
Reconstructions show warmth in the eleventh and early fifteenth centuries, though the twentieth century was warmer still.
Evidence does not show globally synchronous warmth, so the term has limited use for hemispheric or global trends.
The warmth may have sent extra fresh water into the North Atlantic, possibly disrupting ocean circulation ahead of the Little Ice Age.

facts.text: In 1257 Samalas, on the Indonesian island of Lombok, erupted catastrophically with a VEI of 7, one of the Holocene's largest eruptions.
Eruption columns rose 38–43 km; pyroclastic flows buried much of Lombok, destroyed the city of Pamatan and left the 6–7 km Segara Anak caldera.
Ice cores worldwide record a large sulfate spike; the aerosols caused a volcanic winter, cooling by about 0.7 °C in 1258 and 1.2 °C in 1259.
Cold, wet weather brought floods, crop failures and famine in Europe and Japan in 1258–1259, though the scale of the anomalies is still debated.
It may have helped trigger the Little Ice Age; global sea level dipped afterwards, recovering between 1250 and 1400.

conflicts.note: 1257 most likely; 1258 also possible

facts.text: After 14,000 years of dormancy, Quilotoa in Ecuador produced its 1280 Plinian eruption, rated VEI 6.
Collapse left a 3 km caldera; pyroclastic flows and lahars reached the Pacific, and ash spread across the northern Andes.
With Samalas, it is linked to a cold, dry interval on the South American Altiplano between 1200 and 1450.

facts.text: A period of regional cooling, strongest around the North Atlantic, ran from about 1300 to about 1850; it was not a true global ice age.
Hemispherically it was a modest Northern Hemisphere cooling of under 1 °C relative to late twentieth-century levels.
Mountain glaciers advanced in Europe, Alaska, New Zealand and Patagonia; Atlantic pack ice grew from about 1250, though regional maxima came at different times.
Proposed causes include volcanism, low solar activity, ocean circulation changes and human depopulation; climate models point to volcanism as the main driver.
Onset was between 1200 and 1400 in the north and about two centuries later in the south; it ended in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century.

title: Last West Indian giant tortoise dies out

facts.text: Chelonoidis alburyorum, the last West Indian giant tortoise, lasted on the Abacos to 1170 CE, Grand Turk to 1200 and Middle Caicos to about 1400.

title: Moa hunted to extinction in New Zealand

facts.text: Moa, nine species of wingless birds up to about 3.6 m tall, were New Zealand's largest land animals and dominant herbivores until the Māori arrived.
Hunting, and to a lesser degree forest clearance, wiped them out, probably within 100 years of human settlement.
By 1445 all moa were gone, along with Haast's eagle, the giant raptor that had preyed on them.
Middens hold huge numbers of moa bones; ovens near the Waitaki River mouth alone held an estimated 29,000–90,000 birds.

facts.text: An undocumented eruption in 1452/1453, possibly at Kuwae in Vanuatu, is known mainly from its climate signal; one table rates it VEI 7.
It triggered a second pulse of Little Ice Age cooling; Central Europe had seven cold summers in the 1450s.
With Samalas and Tambora, it was among the strongest cooling events of the last millennium.

facts.text: From the 1560s to the 1630s, glaciers at Grindelwald, Switzerland, expanded markedly, part of a worldwide glacial expansion.
Temperatures ran 1–2 °C below twentieth-century averages, among the lowest of the Holocene.
Eruptions of Colima (1585), Nevado del Ruiz (1595) and Huaynaputina (1600) likely contributed, though cooling began about 15 years before the first.
On 19 February 1600 Huaynaputina in southern Peru began the largest eruption ever witnessed in South America, rated VEI 6.
It killed perhaps 1,000–1,500 people, buried the surrounding land under 2 m of volcanic rock and coated nearby El Misti in ash.
Its sulfur cut sunlight by about 1.9 W/m²; the summer of 1601 was among the Northern Hemisphere's coldest of the last six centuries.
Frosts and harvest failures followed from Sweden to China and Japan, probably including Russia's famine of 1601–1603.
With Samalas and the 1452/1453 eruption, it may have helped bring on the Little Ice Age's coldest phase.

title: Atmospheric CO2 dips around 1610

facts.text: Atmospheric carbon dioxide fell around 1610; mass deaths in the Americas after European arrival may explain it, though Huaynaputina's eruption may have contributed.
Conquest and disease killed as many as 90% of Indigenous Americans, and around 50 million hectares of farmland may have returned to forest.
Regrowth of tropical American forests from 1500 to 1650 may have stored 2–5 Pg of carbon; the CO2 drop shows at Law Dome, Antarctica.
Critics argue pre-Columbian farming did not clear forest on a modern scale, so regrowth should have had little effect.
A 2015 report suggested 1610 as one possible start of the Anthropocene.

contested_note: Whether depopulation and reforestation in the Americas caused the CO2 drop is debated; critics doubt the scale of earlier clearing.

title: Last wild aurochs dies in Poland

facts.text: The aurochs, wild ancestor of most modern cattle, once ranged across Eurasia, North Africa and India; only the European form survived into historical times.
Hunting, forest clearance, competition with livestock and cattle diseases left one herd in Poland's Jaktorów forest, where the last died in 1627.

sources.title: List of European species extinct in the Holocene

facts.text: From 1645 to 1715 solar activity was very low, the Maunder Minimum: sunspots were minimal and carbon-14 and beryllium-10 deposition rose.
It fell in the coldest part of the Little Ice Age; one of three especially cold intervals began about 1650.
Northern Hemisphere cooling began before the minimum, and climate models make volcanism the larger driver.
The dodo, a large, flightless relative of pigeons found only on Mauritius, was last seen in 1662 and may have vanished from the main island by the 1640s.
Sailors ate many, but introduced pigs and other species likely did more harm; the dodo became an early poster species for human-caused extinction.
Other Mascarene birds followed, including the Réunion rail (last recorded 1674), Rodrigues rail (1726) and Réunion ibis (1763).

facts.text: Around 9 pm on 26 January 1700, a magnitude 9.0 earthquake ruptured the 1,000 km Cascadia subduction zone off North America's Pacific coast.
Coasts from British Columbia to Oregon dropped up to 2 m and were buried by tsunami sand, leaving drowned 'ghost forests'.
Its tsunami crossed the Pacific and struck Honshu, Japan, about ten hours later, where it was recorded as an 'orphan tsunami'.
Oral traditions of several coastal peoples recall earthquakes and saltwater floods; it remains the zone's last megathrust earthquake.
Drowned red cedars in Oregon and Washington have outermost rings from 1699, the last growing season before the earthquake.

facts.text: Since about 1750 atmospheric methane rose from 722 ppb to 1,936 ppb by 2025, a 2.6-fold increase to the highest level in at least 800,000 years.
Human activities caused almost all of the rise; methane is 3% of greenhouse emissions by mass but about 23% of climate forcing.
After a decade of near-zero growth, methane began climbing again in 2007, with sharp rises in 2015–2019 and a record annual jump in 2021.
Isotopes suggest recent growth comes mainly from microbial sources such as wetlands and agriculture rather than fossil fuels.
From 2010 to 2019 methane caused about 0.5 °C, roughly 30%, of observed global warming.

facts.text: On 1 November 1755 the Great Lisbon earthquake struck, one of the most destructive in history, killing around 100,000 people.
It heads the list of large earthquakes and tsunamis the Azores–Gibraltar fault zone has produced since records began in the 1700s.

title: Steller's sea cow hunted to extinction

facts.text: Steller's sea cow, the largest known sirenian at up to 10 m and 5–10 tonnes, survived as a relict in the Bering Sea's Commander Islands.
Discovered in 1741, it was hunted for meat and hides until it was gone by 1768, just 27 years later.

sources.title: List of Asian species extinct in the Holocene

title: Industrial Revolution starts the greenhouse gas rise

facts.text: With the Industrial Revolution, around 1780 and the steam engine, large-scale greenhouse gas emissions began to warm Earth.
Carbon dioxide had stayed near 280 ppm for 10,000 years before the mid-18th century; it has since risen 54%.
Antarctic ice cores record the highest greenhouse gas levels from the Industrial Revolution on; the IPCC takes 1750 as its pre-industrial baseline.
Warm decades became more common, and recorded extinctions mounted: over 322 species are often cited as lost to humans since then.
It is one proposed start of the Anthropocene, though humans had already reshaped much of Earth's landscape.

facts.text: From June 1783 to February 1784 the 40 km Laki fissure in Iceland poured out about 15 km³ of lava, one of history's largest effusive eruptions.
Its lava fields cover 565 km² of southeast Iceland.
In Northern Hemisphere ice cores its sulfate signal exceeds even Samalas's, and the sulfur caused substantial cooling.
Fluorine and chlorine poisoning devastated farming, and about a fifth of Iceland's people died.
It released about 120 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide; famine cost Egypt a sixth of its people in 1784, and hardship in Europe may have fed the French Revolution.
In April 1815 Tambora, on Sumbawa in Indonesia, produced the most powerful eruption in recorded history, a VEI 7 that ejected 37–45 km³ of material.
Its climax on 10 April drove a column 45 km high; it is the most recent confirmed VEI-7 eruption.
About 10,000–11,000 people died directly, and 49,000–90,000 more from famine and disease on Sumbawa, Lombok and Bali.
Its sulfur dioxide formed a stratospheric sulfate veil, seen in 1815 as a persistent 'dry fog' that dimmed the Sun.

conflicts.note: Start of the eruptive episode; climax April 1815

facts.text: Tambora's aerosols lowered global temperatures by about 0.4–0.7 °C, and 1816 became the 'Year Without a Summer' across the Northern Hemisphere.
Frost and snow struck New England and Quebec in June 1816, ruining most North American crops.
Harvests failed across Europe in the worst famine of the nineteenth century; India's monsoon failed and a new cholera strain spread from Bengal.
1816 was the Northern Hemisphere's second-coldest year since about 1400 and the 1810s the coldest decade on record, aided by an eruption around 1809.
It also fell during the Dalton Minimum, a period of unusually low solar radiation.
A high-magnitude explosive eruption in the northern summer of 1831 may have come from Zavaritski Caldera on Simushir, in the Kuril Islands.
Its reconstructed radiative forcing matches Pinatubo's in 1991 and may explain cooling in 1831–1833, ending the volcanic cold spell of 1809–1831.

title: Glaciers retreat as the Little Ice Age ends

facts.text: Glaciers began a strong retreat after about 1850, as the Little Ice Age ended in the late nineteenth century.
Since 1850 Austria has lost 40% of its glacier cover and Switzerland 30%; Pyrenean glaciers have also retreated greatly.
Alpine glaciers shrank from 1,817 km² in 1876 to 1,342 km² by 1973, reducing river run-off.
By 1879 the ice of Alaska's Glacier Bay had retreated 77 km.
Photographs show glaciers retreating markedly since 1850; only 27% of Glacier National Park's 1850 ice cover remained by 1993.
Sea level was nearly stable for the last 3,000 years until its rise accelerated, an onset variously dated between 1850 and 1900.
Tide gauges, later joined by satellites, show global mean sea level rose 19.5 cm between 1870 and 2004, about 1.44 mm a year.
Between 1901 and 2018 global sea level rose 15–25 cm, faster than in any century for at least 4,000 years, climbing 2.3 mm a year since the 1970s.
On 26–27 August 1883 Krakatoa, in Indonesia's Sunda Strait, exploded in one of history's most violent eruptions, VEI 6, ejecting about 25 km³ of rock.
The blasts were heard 4,800 km away on Rodrigues, and the pressure wave was recorded on barographs worldwide seven times.
Tsunamis with a 41 m run-up killed at least 36,417 people, and two-thirds of the island was destroyed, leaving a caldera.
Ash rose 80 km, and Northern Hemisphere summer temperatures fell by an average of 0.4 °C that year.
The sterilised islands became a classic case of ecosystems rebuilding from scratch; Anak Krakatau rose from the caldera from 1927.

title: Extinction rates soar above background levels

facts.text: Since 1900, extinctions have run at over 1,000 times the background rate, and the rate is still rising.
Humanity has entered what is sometimes called Earth's sixth major extinction, at perhaps 100 to 1,000 times the background rate, though the exact rate is disputed.
Over 322 species are often cited as lost to human activity since the Industrial Revolution, perhaps 500 vertebrates alone, mostly after 1900.
Islands suffer most: 95% of bird extinctions since the late 15th century were of island species.
In October 1902 Santa María in Guatemala had its first recorded eruption, a VEI 6 that ejected about 5.5 km³ of magma over two days.
It ranks with Novarupta (1912) and Pinatubo (1991) among the three largest eruptions of the 20th century; 7,000–13,000 people died.
On 30 June 1908 a huge explosion over the Siberian taiga near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River flattened about 2,150 km² of forest.
Scientists attribute it to the air burst of a 50–60 m meteoroid 5–10 km up, releasing about 10–15 megatons; whether asteroid or comet is debated.
The shock wave killed at least three people and was detected worldwide; bright nights followed across western Eurasia.
Models suggest it made nitric oxide that cut ozone by 35–45% in early 1909 and tripled ground UV-B at 30°N.
It is the most violent impact event recorded in modern times; nearby Lake Cheko may be a fragment's crater, though sediment studies disagree.

facts.text: Beginning 6 June 1912, Novarupta on the Alaska Peninsula produced the 20th century's largest eruption, a 60-hour VEI 6 blast of 13–15 km³ of ash.
Magma drained from beneath Mount Katmai, whose summit collapsed; deep pyroclastic flows filled the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes.
No one died directly, but the most ash-buried Native villages were abandoned.
The passenger pigeon, once perhaps 40% of all birds in North America, was destroyed by habitat loss and mass hunting for a meat industry.
It was declared extinct in 1914 when Martha, the last known bird, died at the Cincinnati Zoo, 20 years after the species vanished from the wild.
The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, a dog-like marsupial predator, survived only in Tasmania; the last confirmed wild one was killed in 1931.
The last known thylacine died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936, though a 2023 analysis of sightings suggests it lingered for decades.

sources.title: List of Australia-New Guinea species extinct in the Holocene

facts.text: On 12 February 1947 an iron meteorite of over 23 tonnes fell in the Sikhote-Alin Mountains of the Soviet Far East.
Its fragments scattered over about 1.3 km² and blasted craters up to 26 m across.

title: Atlantic overturning circulation weakens

facts.text: Reconstructions suggest that by 2015 the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation was weaker than before the Industrial Revolution, by roughly 15–20% since the mid-twentieth century.
One analysis found it weaker in 1975–1995 than at any time in the past millennium; another estimates a slowdown of 0.46 sverdrups per decade since 1950.
Ocean warming and Greenland meltwater may be weakening it, but some studies find no overall decline, and the share of natural variability is debated.

contested_note: Reconstructions show weakening, but observations and some analyses find no clear decline, and how much is due to climate change rather than natural variability is debated.

facts.text: Average ocean-surface pH fell from about 8.15 to 8.05 between 1950 and 2026, roughly a 26% rise in hydrogen-ion concentration.
Human carbon dioxide is the main cause: from 1850 to 2022 the ocean absorbed 26% of all anthropogenic emissions.
Present-day surface pH, and its rate of change, are unprecedented for at least 26,000 years.
Interior ocean pH has also fallen everywhere over the last 20–30 years, and open-ocean surface pH has dropped about 0.017–0.027 units per decade since the late 1980s.
Falling pH lowers carbonate saturation, speeding dissolution of the calcium carbonate that molluscs, foraminifera and other shell-builders need.

title: Rapid global warming since the mid-20th century

facts.text: Greenhouse gases from fossil fuels have caused planetary-scale climate change; warm decades became ever more common after the Industrial Revolution.
The global average temperature was 14 °C for 1951–1980 and 15 °C for 2013–2017.
The ocean is about 0.7 °C warmer than in 1950, warming that has contributed more than 15 cm of sea-level rise.
The Arctic warmed faster than most regions and land twice as fast as ocean; Antarctica warmed after 1957, the South Pole at triple the global rate after 1990.
Effects include more extreme weather, thawing permafrost, marine heatwaves, ocean deoxygenation and acidification.

facts.text: A magnitude 9.0 megathrust earthquake struck off Kamchatka, one of the four most powerful quakes measured since the 1930s.
It ruptured the Kuril–Kamchatka subduction zone, which has produced several giant quakes, including those of 1737 and 2025.
Just after the quake, Tao-Rusyr Caldera in the Kuril Islands had its only historical eruption, building a small lava dome.
On 5 November 1952 the Mw 8.8–9.0 quake raised a tsunami that struck the Kuril Islands and Kamchatka, with waves 15–18 m high at Severo-Kurilsk.
It remains Russia's most powerful recorded earthquake, fifth worldwide since 1900, and Russia's deadliest and most damaging tsunami.
After World War II, population, economic growth, pollution and resource use all began rising at a dramatic rate, the so-called Great Acceleration.
Since about 1950 humans have doubled Earth's fixed nitrogen, opened an ozone hole with CFCs, and cut off almost a fifth of river sediment from the sea.
Atomic-bomb tests scattered radionuclides such as caesium-137, strontium-90 and plutonium around the globe, embedding them in sediments and glacial ice.
Sediments of Crawford Lake, Ontario, record a plutonium spike from hydrogen-bomb tests at 1952, with carbon particles and nitrates from fossil fuels and fertilizers.
Global radionuclide levels peaked around 1965, and bomb carbon-14 entered atmospheric CO2 and the biosphere.

title: West Antarctic Ice Sheet warms and loses ice

facts.text: West Antarctica warmed by about 2.4 °C between 1958 and 2012, a change attributed to rising greenhouse gases.
Warming seawater melts its ice shelves, and coastal glaciers, above all Thwaites, Pine Island and Smith, have retreated substantially since at least the 1990s.
Ice loss rose from 53 Gt a year in 1992 to 159 Gt a year in 2017, adding about 7.6 mm to global sea level.

title: Mauna Loa records rising CO2 (Keeling Curve)

facts.text: Continuous measurements on Mauna Loa from March 1958 gave the first significant evidence of rapidly rising atmospheric carbon dioxide.
CO2 climbed steadily from 313 ppm in March 1958 to 406 ppm in November 2018, by then rising about 2.5 ppm a year.
Air in ice cores shows Holocene CO2 stayed between 275 and 285 ppm until it began rising sharply early in the nineteenth century.
The accelerating rise comes from burning fossil fuels; the curve also swings about 6 ppm each year with Northern Hemisphere plant growth.
On 9 May 2013 daily CO2 at Mauna Loa passed 400 ppm, a level probably not reached since the mid-Pliocene, 2 to 4 million years ago.

facts.text: The largest earthquake ever recorded, of moment magnitude 9.4–9.6, struck southern Chile on 22 May 1960.
It ruptured the subduction zone where the Nazca plate sinks beneath southern Chile, a boundary with a long history of massive earthquakes.
Two days after the main shock, the Cordón Caulle volcano began erupting along its southern flank.
Its tsunami reached 25 m on the Chilean coast and 10.7 m at Hilo, Hawaii, 10,000 km away; between 1,000 and 6,000 people died.
Similar great earthquakes struck the region in 1575 and around 1800 BC, the latter dated from tsunami debris in the Atacama Desert.
A magnitude 9.2 megathrust earthquake struck southern Alaska, one of the four most powerful recorded since the 1930s.
The shaking collapsed weak clay beds left by ancient Lake Atna, setting off catastrophic landslides in Anchorage.
Its seismic waves set water sloshing in seiches as far away as Puerto Rico.
Lasting 4 minutes 38 seconds, the Mw 9.2–9.3 quake is the most powerful recorded in North America and second worldwide since 1900.
Land rose across 520,000 km², by 13–15 m on Montague Island; tsunamis ran up 67 m, and about 139 people died.

verification.place: The 1964 Prince William Sound, Alaska Earthquake

facts.text: Monitored vertebrate wildlife populations fell by almost 70% on average after 1970, driven mainly by agriculture and fishing.
Land-use change, overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species all contributed; migratory freshwater fish declined by 76%.
In 1987 the death of the last Kauaʻi ʻōʻō ended an entire bird family, the Hawaiian honeyeaters.
In the Yangtze, the Chinese paddlefish was last recorded in 2003, and the baiji river dolphin was declared extinct in 2006, the loss of a whole genus.

facts.text: Chytridiomycosis, a fungal disease spread by travel and the wildlife trade, has caused steep declines in over 500 amphibian species and perhaps 90 extinctions.
Victims include Australia's gastric-brooding frogs, gone by the mid-1980s, and Costa Rica's golden toad, last seen in 1989.
The chytrid Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, a main driver of the worldwide amphibian decline, has spread across Australia, New Zealand, Central America and Africa.

title: Arctic sea ice shrinks in the satellite era

facts.text: Arctic sea ice, tracked by satellite since 1979, has declined by over 50%, the loss accelerating to 4.7% per decade in the early 21st century.
The September minimum hit a record 3.39 million km² in 2012, beating the 2007 record of 4.16 million km².
Ice at least four years old fell from 26% of the cover in 1988 to 7% by 2013, and ice thickness dropped 66% over six decades.
Since 1979 the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average, and the melt season has lengthened five days per decade.
Sea ice lost between 1979 and 2011 caused radiative forcing equal to a quarter of CO2 emissions over the same years.
Mount St. Helens erupted catastrophically on 18 May 1980, a VEI 5 event of about 1.2–1.3 km³, the most significant in the contiguous US in recorded history.
Its flank collapsed into a huge debris avalanche, which became the reference case for recognizing collapses at volcanoes such as Mount Bandai and Parinacota.
Ash dusted land from British Columbia to Manitoba, and ferns recolonized the devastated ground first, a 'fern spike' like the one after the dinosaur extinction.

title: Ozone layer thins and the Antarctic ozone hole opens

facts.text: From the late 1970s stratospheric ozone thinned worldwide, with a far deeper springtime loss over the poles, the Antarctic 'ozone hole'.
Manufactured chlorofluorocarbons, halons and related refrigerants, solvents and propellants were the main cause.
Antarctic spring ozone fell by up to 70%, first reported in 1985; inside the polar vortex over half the lower-stratospheric ozone is destroyed each spring.
Mid-latitude total ozone fell below pre-1980 values between 1980 and 1996; Arctic losses reached 30% in the coldest winters and springs.
Stronger ultraviolet-B under depleted ozone cuts plant productivity by about 6%, and the hole has at times reached parts of Australia, Chile and Argentina.

title: El Chichón eruption disturbs northern winters

facts.text: Long-dormant El Chichón in Chiapas, Mexico, produced three Plinian eruptions within a week in spring 1982.
The VEI 5 eruption put 7 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide and 20 million tonnes of particles into the stratosphere, which circled Earth in three weeks.
Its aerosols brought winter warming to North America, Europe and Siberia in 1982–83, while Alaska, Greenland and China ran colder than normal.
Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted on 15 June 1991, a VEI 6 event and the second-largest land eruption of the 20th century after Novarupta in 1912.
Its ash column rose 35 km, and it put more particles into the stratosphere than any eruption since Krakatoa in 1883.
Aerosols spread a global sulfuric-acid haze; world temperatures fell about 0.5 °C in 1991–1993, and ozone depletion temporarily rose sharply.
The summit collapsed into a 2.5 km caldera, later filled by Lake Pinatubo, and rain-driven lahars flooded the surrounding lowlands.
It released 17–20 megatonnes of sulfur dioxide, and 1992 brought a 'Summer that Wasn't', with odd weather and cooling across the United States.

title: Sea-level rise accelerates in the satellite era

facts.text: Satellite altimeters, flying since TOPEX/Poseidon in 1992, measured 7.5 cm of rise from 1993 to 2017, and the rate reached 4.62 mm a year in 2013–2022.
From 1993 to 2018, melting ice sheets and glaciers supplied 44% of the rise and thermal expansion of warming seawater 42%.
Greenland's contribution grew from 0.07 mm a year in 1992–1997 to 0.68 mm a year in 2012–2017.
Flooding of Bramble Cay in 2016 wiped out its melomys, the first mammal lost to human-caused sea-level rise, declared extinct in 2019.
Jakobshavn Isbræ, Greenland's largest outlet glacier, switched to rapid mass loss after 1997 as warming North Atlantic water melted glacier fronts from below.
Annual ice loss from the whole sheet accelerated to about 187 Gt in 2000–2010 and 286 Gt in 2010–2018.
In July 2012 melt reached 97% of the ice sheet's surface, a melt unmatched since 1889, and that year's net loss of 464 Gt set a record.
An even larger melt in 2019 brought a record net loss of 586 Gt, with about 600 Gt of ice lost in just two months.
During another record melt in 2021, rain fell for 13 hours at the 3,216 m Summit Station, where it had never rained before.
In 1998 the first globally recognized coral bleaching event struck, with 21% of reefs under bleaching-level heat stress.
A very strong 1997–98 El Niño drove it, warming Indian Ocean waters by 2 °C; 1998 became the warmest year then on record.
Belize's barrier reef had its first recorded mass bleaching, and the Great Barrier Reef its first major bleaching event.
Mass bleaching has grown sharply in frequency and severity worldwide since the early 1980s, driven by marine heatwaves.

title: Global warming 'hiatus', 1998–2013

facts.text: From 1998 to 2013, negative phases of the Pacific decadal and Atlantic multidecadal oscillations briefly slowed surface warming.
The slowdown is less pronounced in current observational datasets than in those available in 2012.
It ended after 2012: every year from 2015 on was warmer than any before, and 2024 exceeded 1.5 °C.

contested_note: The slowdown is less pronounced in newer datasets, and the media claim that warming 'stopped in 1998' is disputed.

title: Mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef

facts.text: Marine heatwaves caused mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef in 1998, 2002, 2006, 2016, 2017 and 2020, with another event confirmed in March 2022.
Over half of the reef's coral cover was lost between 1995 and 2017, and many breeding adults died in the 2016–17 bleaching.
Warming is already bleaching coral reefs worldwide, habitats that sustain high biodiversity.
On 26 December 2004 the boundary between the Indian and Burma plates slipped off Sumatra in a megathrust earthquake of magnitude 9.1–9.3.
More than 1,600 km of the fault ruptured, lifting the seafloor up to 5 m and shifting it 11 m sideways within seven minutes.
The tsunami reached 35 m near Banda Aceh and killed approximately 229,800 people around the Indian Ocean.
The second- or third-most powerful quake since 1900, it released about one-eighth of all seismic moment from 1906 to 2005.
Deposits on Phra Thong, Thailand, record at least three earlier major tsunamis in 2,800 years, the latest about 700 years ago.
A magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck central Chile on 27 February 2010.
Its waves set off seiches as far away as Louisiana, and the Caldera del Atuel and other volcanic centres subsided after the quake.
On 11 March 2011 a magnitude 9.0–9.1 undersea megathrust earthquake struck off Honshu, as the Pacific plate subducted beneath the Okhotsk microplate.
It ranks among the four most powerful earthquakes measured since the 1930s, and the worst-hit areas of Tōhoku shook for about six minutes.
Its seismic waves crossed 8,000 km in under 30 minutes, raising seiches about 1.5–1.8 m high in Norway.
Its tsunami reached up to 40.5 m at Miyako and swept up to 10 km inland; 19,759 people died, and three Fukushima Daiichi reactors melted down.
Japan's most powerful recorded quake, it released about 93% of the moment estimated to have built up there since 1926.
On 15 February 2013 an asteroid about 20 m across exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in an airburst of around 500 kilotons.
The largest airburst observed with modern instruments, it shattered windows, injured over 1,000 people and scattered meteorites.
Its similar dynamics reinforced the view that the Tunguska blast was a meteoroid exploding high in the air.
Record ocean heat during the 2014–2017 El Niño caused the longest and most destructive coral bleaching event then known.
Bleaching in 2014–2016 killed coral on an unprecedented scale; reefs making up three-quarters of the world's reef systems were severely bleached.
In 2016 bleaching killed 29 to 50% of the Great Barrier Reef's coral; near Port Douglas over half the bleached corals died.

title: Reykjanes Peninsula volcanism resumes after 800 years

facts.text: After nearly 800 years of quiet, volcanic and earthquake activity resumed on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula from 2020; Fagradalsfjall erupted on 19 March 2021.
A 15 km magma intrusion in late 2023 opened a subsiding graben beneath Grindavík, forcing the town's evacuation; nine Sundhnúkur fissure eruptions followed through August 2025.
The eruptions were small and effusive (VEI 1), but experts suggested the activity may mark the start of decades of volcanism.

verification.note: GVP's Reykjanes record begins with the 2023 eruptions; the event's range starts with the 2020 renewal of activity.

title: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai eruption
article: 2022 Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai eruption and tsunami

facts.text: After erupting from December 2021, the submarine Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai volcano exploded on 15 January 2022, the largest eruption since Pinatubo, rated at least VEI 5.
Its plume reached 58 km into the mesosphere, and the blast, the largest atmospheric explosion recorded by modern instruments, sent pressure waves around the globe.
It lofted 146 million tons of seawater, a tenth of the stratosphere's water vapour, enough to warm Earth's surface temporarily; a Pacific-wide tsunami followed.

sources.title: 2022 Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai eruption and tsunami

conflicts.note: Start of the eruptive episode; climax 14-15 January 2022

facts.text: A fourth global coral bleaching event began in February 2023; in April 2024 NOAA confirmed it as the largest yet.
From January 2023 to September 2025 bleaching-level heat reached about 84% of the world's reef area, with bleaching in at least 83 countries and territories.
Great Barrier Reef hard-coral cover fell by up to 30.6% from 2024 to 2025, the largest single-year drops since 1986 in two regions.

title: 2024 is the warmest year on record

facts.text: 2024 was the warmest year since regular tracking began in 1850, at +1.60 °C, well above the 1.5 °C mark.
It followed 2023, already 1.48 °C above the 1850–1900 average and declared the warmest year on record as soon as it ended.
The years 2015–2025 included all eleven warmest since 1850, and the 2016–2025 decade averaged 1.26 °C above pre-industrial.
The global ocean was the warmest ever recorded in 2022.
NOAA data rank 2025 as the third-warmest year on record, behind 2024 and 2023.

title: Anthropocene epoch proposal rejected

facts.text: In 2024, after 15 years of deliberation, stratigraphers voted down by a wide margin the proposal to make the Anthropocene a formal epoch after the Holocene.
Its shallow sediment record and very recent start date weighed against it; the ICS and IUGS then confirmed the rejection by a near-unanimous vote.
The term stays in wide informal use for human impact on the Earth system, though its validity as a scientific term remains disputed.

contested_note: The Anthropocene was rejected as a formal epoch in March 2024 and criticized in 2026 journal commentary, with no formal reopening; the term's validity remains disputed.

facts.text: In 2025 another giant megathrust earthquake, of magnitude 8.8, struck the Kamchatka coast, where the Pacific plate subducts along the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench.
